transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What has been bothering you lately that made you decide to come in today?

Um, yeah… thanks for seeing me. I guess it’s mostly that I’ve been spending a lot more time than I should checking things. Like dressing supplies, door locks, file dimensions, revision notes—things like that.

I know some checking is normal, and I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, but I can kind of lose hours to it. I’ll feel like I can’t really move on until I’ve gone through the same routine enough times that the anxiety settles down. Does that make sense?
Right before you start checking, do you usually get any intrusive, unwanted thoughts or mental images about something bad happening if you don’t check, that feel hard to dismiss?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I don’t want to overstate it, because sometimes it’s just a feeling more than a clear picture, but… even after I know I cleaned the wound area or reviewed a CAD file, this thought kind of cuts in like, “What if you missed one tiny thing?”

And then it jumps to something bad, like an infection happening, or a design mistake that could hurt someone. I can tell myself I already checked it and that it’s probably fine, but it doesn’t really… land, I guess. It’s hard to dismiss until I check again. Does that answer what you mean?

How much are these checking routines and the anxiety around them actually getting in the way of your day-to-day life—for example, making you late, interfering with work, or stopping you from doing things you want to do?

Yeah… it is starting to affect things, more than I’d like to admit, probably.

At work, I’m still getting things done, but project deadlines have started slipping because I’ll stay late going over files or notes until I feel comfortable enough to actually submit them. I know that’s not ideal.

And outside of work, it’s… I guess I’ve let some stuff go. I’ve stopped making it to paddleboarding meetups and workouts sometimes because the routines take up the time I used to keep for myself. I don’t mean to make it sound dramatic, but it’s definitely getting in the way.
Outside of these specific checking situations, do you find yourself feeling anxious or worrying excessively about lots of different everyday things, even when nothing in particular has gone wrong?

Um… I don’t think so? Not in a broad, all-the-time way.

I mean, I get stressed like anyone, but it doesn’t feel like I’m worrying about everything across the board. It’s more tied to those specific situations where I feel responsible for catching something. Outside of that, I’m usually okay, I think. Does that distinction make sense?
Over the past few weeks, have you been feeling down or sad most of the day on most days, even at times when you’re not caught up in the checking or anxiety about mistakes?

I don’t think so, no. I mean, I get pretty frustrated with myself sometimes, and worn out, but I wouldn’t say I’ve been sad most of the day most days.

When I’m not stuck in that whole checking loop, my mood is usually okay. Maybe not perfect, but not like… persistently down, if that’s what you mean. Does that sound like I’m answering it correctly?

When you catch yourself going back to re-check things, does any part of you feel like, "This is over the top and doesn’t really make sense, but I still feel driven to do it," or does it mostly feel like the careful and correct way to do things?

Yeah… honestly, I think part of me does know it’s over the top.

I try to tell myself I’m just being careful, and sometimes it really does feel like the responsible thing to do. But when I’m checking the same dressing supplies, or the door lock, or file dimensions and revision notes over and over… I know, at least intellectually, that I’ve already checked it.

It’s just that I don’t feel like I’m allowed to move on until I’ve done the routine enough times that the anxiety drops. That probably sounds a little excessive, I know. But in the moment it feels hard to stop.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports recurrent intrusive doubts about having missed small but potentially harmful mistakes (e.g., infection risk, design errors) that lead to repeated checking of locks, dressing supplies, and work files until anxiety decreases. They recognize the behavior as excessive and irrational, yet feel driven to perform it. The checking consumes hours, delays work deadlines, and interferes with leisure activities, indicating clinically significant impairment. There is no evidence of pervasive, free‑floating anxiety or persistent depressed mood. This presentation is most consistent with obsessive–compulsive disorder (F42). Generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) is considered but less likely given the circumscribed, obsession-linked nature of the anxiety and the presence of clear compulsions.
